title: What is a recursive program — explain the base case, the recursive case, and the difference between direct, indirect, and tail recursion?
shortTitle: What is a recursive program (base case, recursive case, direct/indirect/tail recursion)?

s1_definition.profdef: Recursion is a technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive method needs a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that moves toward the base case. Direct recursion is a method calling itself; indirect recursion is method A calling method B which calls A again; tail recursion is when the recursive call is the very last operation, which some languages optimize but the standard Java virtual machine does not.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh at National Bank of India wants the total of a stack of monthly statements. He looks at the top statement, remembers its amount, and then hands the rest of the stack back to himself to total again. He keeps doing this until the stack is empty, which is the moment he stops. Emptying the stack one statement at a time, handing the remainder back to yourself each time, is recursion. The empty stack is the base case that tells him to stop; taking one off and recursing on the rest is the recursive case.
s1_definition.oneliner: Recursion is a method calling itself on a smaller input, and it must always have a base case to stop and a recursive case that shrinks the problem toward that base case.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Recursion is a technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive method needs a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that moves toward the base case. Direct recursion is a method calling itself; indirect recursion is method A calling method B which calls A again; tail recursion is when the recursive call is the very last operation, which some languages optimize but the standard Java virtual machine does not.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh at National Bank of India wants the total of a stack of monthly statements. He looks at the top statement, remembers its amount, and then hands the rest of the stack back to himself to total again. He keeps doing this until the stack is empty, which is the moment he stops. Emptying the stack one statement at a time, handing the remainder back to yourself each time, is recursion. The empty stack is the base case that tells him to stop; taking one off and recursing on the rest is the recursive case.

**One line to remember:** Recursion is a method calling itself on a smaller input, and it must always have a base case to stop and a recursive case that shrinks the problem toward that base case.

sections.s2_technical:
A recursive method has two mandatory parts. The base case is the condition under which the method returns a value directly without calling itself, and it is what prevents infinite recursion. The recursive case is where the method calls itself with arguments that are strictly closer to the base case, so the chain of calls eventually terminates. If you forget the base case, or the recursive case never actually shrinks the problem, you get infinite recursion that fills the call stack and throws a `StackOverflowError`.

Each recursive call creates a new stack frame on the thread's call stack. That frame stores the method's local variables, parameters, and the return address. For a factorial of five, there are five frames stacked up before the base case returns, and then they unwind one by one. For example, computing the compound growth of a deposit over several years can be expressed recursively: `balance(year) = balance(year - 1).multiply(rate)` with the base case `balance(0) = principal`. Here is a small banking example: `BigDecimal interestFor(int months) { if (months == 0) return principal; return interestFor(months - 1).add(interestFor(months - 1).multiply(monthlyRate)); }` where `months == 0` is the base case.

Direct recursion is the common form where a method calls itself, like `factorial` calling `factorial`. Indirect recursion is when method A calls method B, and B calls A, forming a cycle; an example is an `isEven(n)` that calls `isOdd(n - 1)` while `isOdd(n)` calls `isEven(n - 1)`. Tail recursion is a special shape where the recursive call is the last thing the method does, with nothing left to compute after it returns, for example `int sum(int n, int acc) { if (n == 0) return acc; return sum(n - 1, acc + n); }`. Some languages optimize tail calls into a loop so they use constant stack space, but a senior-level point is that the standard Java virtual machine does not perform tail-call optimization, so even tail-recursive Java can overflow the stack on very deep input. For that reason, in production banking code I convert deep recursion into an iterative loop or use an explicit stack when the depth is unbounded, and I keep recursion for naturally bounded, shallow problems like walking a small account hierarchy.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India lets a customer like Rajesh open a parent savings account that can have sub-accounts, and each sub-account can itself have sub-accounts, forming a tree. To compute the total balance across the whole tree, we cannot write a fixed number of loops because the depth is not known in advance. This is exactly what recursion solves, because the method can call itself on each child sub-account no matter how deep the tree goes.

Problem 2 — The bank also computes a simple month-by-month projected balance for a recurring deposit. The balance in any month depends on the balance of the previous month, which is a naturally recursive definition. This is exactly how a recursive case with a base case works, because month zero is the known starting principal and every later month is defined in terms of the month before it.

In the mini-project we build an `AccountNode` tree, a `BalanceCalculator` with a direct-recursive `totalBalance` method, a tail-recursive `projectMonths` helper, and a short indirect-recursion demonstration. The main demo builds Rajesh's account tree, sums it recursively, and projects Priya's deposit forward a few months, logging each step.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's account tree with root balance 1,000,000, a salary sub-account of 50,000, a savings sub-account of 200,000, and a nested fixed deposit of 75,000. Priya's balance is 250,000 projected three months at one percent.

Step 1: The main method builds the tree and calls `totalBalance(root)`. The data is the root `AccountNode`, and nothing has changed yet.

Step 2: `totalBalance` reads the root balance of 1,000,000 into a local sum. The sum lives in this stack frame only.

Step 3: For the first child, the salary node, the method calls itself. A new stack frame is created. That child has no children, so it hits the leaf path and returns 50,000. The frame unwinds and sum becomes 1,050,000.

Step 4: For the second child, the savings node, a new frame is created with its own balance of 200,000. It has one child, the nested fixed deposit, so it recurses again into a third frame that returns 75,000. The savings frame returns 275,000, and the root sum becomes 1,325,000.

Step 5: Control returns to main with the final total of 1,325,000. Then `projectMonths` runs with Priya's 250,000, growing one percent each month across three tail-recursive calls, returning roughly 257,575.25.

```text
[INFO] Rajesh tree total balance Rs.1325000
[INFO] Priya projected after 3 months at 1% = Rs.257575.250000
[INFO] Is 4 even (indirect recursion)? true
```

    Post: returns node balance + sum of all descendant balances

    1. read own balance into sum
    2. for each child → recurse (new stack frame)
    3. child returns → add to sum
    4. return sum (frame unwinds)

sections.s6_takeaway:
Recursion is a technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that same problem. Every correct recursive method has two parts that I always make sure are present. The first is the base case, which is the condition where the method returns a value directly without recursing, and this is what stops the recursion. The second is the recursive case, where the method calls itself with arguments that are strictly closer to the base case, so the chain of calls is guaranteed to end. If I forget the base case, or my recursive case never actually shrinks the problem, the call stack keeps growing until it throws a StackOverflowError.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I used recursion where the structure was naturally recursive and bounded. A good example is an account that can own sub-accounts, and each sub-account can own further sub-accounts, forming a tree of unknown depth. To total the balance across the whole tree I cannot write a fixed number of loops, so I wrote a method that reads the current node's balance and then calls itself on each child, adding up what each subtree returns. This is direct recursion, the most common form, where a method calls itself.

There are three flavors I distinguish in an interview. Direct recursion is a method calling itself. Indirect recursion is when method A calls method B and B calls A again, forming a cycle, like an isEven method that defers to an isOdd method and back again. Tail recursion is a special shape where the recursive call is the very last thing the method does, with nothing left to compute afterward, and in languages that optimize it the compiler turns it into a loop using constant stack space.

The senior nuance I always add is that the standard Java virtual machine does not perform tail-call optimization, so even a tail-recursive method in Java still consumes one stack frame per call and can overflow on very deep input. Because of that, in production code where depth is unbounded, I convert deep recursion into an iterative loop with an explicit stack, or I push the aggregation into the database with a recursive common table expression. I keep recursion for problems that are naturally hierarchical and shallow, like walking a small account tree, because there the code is far clearer and the depth stays safely within the stack.
